solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Will do well, having sons with Scotland Yard?

parts.note: the old surname prefix Fitz- means son of, so several sons are playfully Fitz-es, said the same way
The Bill is British slang for the police, and the name of a long-running TV police drama set in London

explanation.surface: A proud father imagines his boys signing up with the Metropolitan Police.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitz- (as in FitzGerald) means son of, so sons are jokily FITS; Scotland Yard, London's police headquarters, stands for the police, slangily THE BILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: something that suits the purpose exactly is said to meet the requirement, and so will do well.

clue.text: Man in vehicle following one

indicators.note: the vehicle word comes after the one word in the answer

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
a van is a goods vehicle

explanation.surface: A passenger sits in a van behind another vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan is a man's first name, the Russian form of John.

clue.text: Noticed V missing from VII

indicators.note: missing from tells us to take the V out of the spelt-out number

parts.note: VII is seven in Roman numerals, spelt out as the word
the letter V taken as it stands

explanation.surface: Someone spots that a Roman numeral has lost a symbol.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to spell VII out as the English word before removing V.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something noticed has been observed or spotted by the eye.

clue.text: Until I left — leaving to go into Lady's Watches

indicators.note: to go into tells us the trimmed word sits inside the lady's word

parts.note: something that belongs to a lady is hers

indicators.note: leaving means the letters for I and left depart from the word until

parts.note: I taken as written

explanation.surface: A shop sign announces a closing date for a sale on ladies' watches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes I and L out of UNTIL to give UNT, which goes into HERS.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunter is a pocket watch with a hinged cover protecting the glass, so these are kinds of watch.

clue.text: Deep sound in low key, reverberating

indicators.note: reverberating suggests a sound bouncing back, so the letters are read in reverse order

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
B is a musical key

explanation.surface: A bass note in a low key echoes around a hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low' looks like describing pitch, but it is the verb for a cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a boom is a loud, deep, resonant noise, like a foghorn or a cannon.

clue.text: They put up with one — at a price

definitions.text: They put up with one — at a price

parts.words: They put up with one — at a price
parts.note: reads as people tolerating someone for money, but describes paying guests who are given lodging in someone's home

explanation.surface: People grudgingly tolerating an irritating person because they are paid to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' means accommodate, not tolerate: these people stay with a householder and pay rent.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying guests staying in a private house are put up by their landlady in exchange for rent.

clue.text: My turn, mum!

parts.note: in a game, your go is your turn
mum means silent, and sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: A child at a board game insists to their mother that it is their go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation of surprise, not the possessive; 'mum' is the adjective for silent, not a mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, interchangeable as in 'Oh my!' and its equivalent.

clue.text: Tale of a traitor that won't make front-page news?

definitions.text: Tale of a traitor that won't make front-page news?

parts.words: Tale of a traitor that won't make front-page news?
parts.note: a betrayer working from within tells a tale that sits on the inner pages, not the front

explanation.surface: A journalist's scoop about a spy is buried away from the front page.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means a confidential account by someone in the know; the clue also reads it as a story printed inside the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a confidential account of events known only to those involved, such as a mole.

clue.text: Time and time again retreating

indicators.note: again retreating says the same time read backwards still gives that word, as it is a palindrome

parts.note: midday is a time, twelve o'clock

explanation.surface: A soldier's account of falling back over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: The time of day reads the same in either direction, so 'retreating' leaves it unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock midday is a particular time of day.

clue.text: Doesn't matter what an ex-bookie does

definitions.meaning: the idiom means is of no consequence
a bookmaker who has retired no longer sets betting prices

explanation.surface: A retired betting man shrugs off his former trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: when something has no effect on the outcome it is unimportant; a retired bookie literally stops offering prices on bets.

clue.text: Moor speaking an Asian language

indicators.note: speaking signals that the word for moor is to be heard rather than written

parts.note: to moor a boat is to tie it up

explanation.surface: A North African Moor converses in a language from the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' looks like a person (or heathland), but it is the verb for tying up a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The official tongue of Thailand is a language of South-East Asia.

clue.text: Should that be so, where is it packed?

definitions.meaning: asks which box or suitcase holds something

explanation.surface: Someone preparing for a trip asks which bag an item went into.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the phrase introduces a consequence if a condition holds; literally it asks which container something is in.

clue.text: Appalled to see a 'phantom' spelled with 'a' instead of 'o'

indicators.note: the clue spells out that the vowel O in the phantom word is to be replaced by A

parts.note: a phantom is a ghost

explanation.surface: Someone is horrified to find a word misspelt on a page.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone filled with shock and horror is appalled.

clue.text: Yank taking booze back. He's very tight

indicators.note: back tells us the combined letters are read in reverse

parts.note: to yank is to drag or pull hard
gin is a kind of booze

explanation.surface: An American grabs a drink and is drunk as a result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American and 'tight' like drunk; one is a verb, the other means stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser who hates spending is called tight, meaning stingy, in British slang.

clue.text: In blasted love for a man!

indicators.note: In placed first says the love letter goes inside the cursing word

parts.note: blasted and damn are both mild curses meaning confounded
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: An exasperated person curses their love for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Damon is a man's first name, as in the actor Matt Damon.

clue.text: Get cracking — rain's seeping through rock

indicators.note: cracking means breaking apart, so the letters of get and rain are broken up and rearranged together

parts.note: taken as written
the word rain, with seeping through describing it soaking into the other letters as they mix

explanation.surface: A command to hurry, because rain is getting into stonework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get cracking' looks like an order to hurry, but 'cracking' is the anagram signal; 'seeping through' just paints rain mixing into the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Granite is a hard igneous rock used for building and kerbstones.

clue.text: Gather a valley surrounds it

indicators.note: surrounds tells us the valley word goes round the letter a

parts.note: a glen is a narrow valley, especially in Scotland

explanation.surface: A valley encircles something and gathers it in.
explanation.definitionFit: To glean is to gather leftover grain, or information, bit by bit.

clue.text: Strain after naughty child gets hurt

indicators.note: after puts the tune word behind the child word

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
a strain is a tune or melody, an air

explanation.surface: A parent is injured after straining with a badly behaved child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strain' looks like an injury, but it is a melody.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to impair is to damage or weaken, so to hurt.

clue.text: Be sick on board cruises

indicators.note: on, read with board, means within the ship, so the ill word goes inside the ship letters

parts.note: board here stands for a ship, abbreviated SS for steamship, as in 'on board'
to ail is to be ill

explanation.surface: A passenger is seasick during a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords write a ship as SS (steamship); being 'on board' puts letters inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a vessel that cruises over the water sails.

clue.text: Are informed at this point verbally

indicators.note: verbally means by spoken words, so we take the sound of the place word

parts.note: here means at this place or point

explanation.surface: Someone is told news in person at a particular moment.
explanation.definitionFit: When people learn news they are told it, as in 'I hear you've moved'.

clue.text: Turning the spigots makes little difference

indicators.note: turning signals the letters of the spigot word go round the other way

parts.note: spigots are taps

explanation.surface: A plumber notes that adjusting the taps barely changes the flow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little difference' means a minor disagreement, not a slight change.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a petty quarrel, a small difference of opinion.

clue.text: Skeleton found in reef?

parts.note: suggests a shipwreck victim's bones, but describes the hard skeletal material of tiny marine animals that builds reefs

explanation.surface: A diver discovers human bones lodged in a reef.
explanation.definitionFit: Reefs are built from the calcium carbonate skeletons secreted by colonies of tiny polyps.

clue.text: Knock up a score?

parts.note: sounds like scoring runs in sport, but a score is a piece of music to be written

explanation.surface: A batsman quickly makes some runs.
explanation.definitionFit: To write a musical score is to create music, quickly knocking one up.

clue.text: Down the road with former President Reagan

parts.note: late can mean former, as in the late chairman
Ronald Reagan, US President, shortened to Ron

explanation.surface: A road trip with Ronald Reagan after he left office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down the road' means in the future, not along a street.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: down the road means at some future time, eventually.

clue.text: Unfireable, get the picture?

parts.note: something that cannot be set alight will not ignite; the phrase also means understand

explanation.surface: A boss tells an employee they cannot be dismissed, and asks if they understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfireable' means not able to burn, not secure in a job: such material won't ignite.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to understand something eventually is to get the picture.

clue.text: More hostile when it twists in illegal snare

indicators.note: in tells us the twisted pair sits inside the rearranged trap
illegal suggests the trap is improper, so its letters are rearranged
twists means the two letters turn round

explanation.surface: A poacher's illegal trap gets worse when an animal twists in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twists' turns IT to TI, which goes 'in' NASER, the reworked SNARE from 'illegal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Comparative synonym: someone more hostile is more unpleasant or spiteful.

clue.text: May be taken out to have a drink somewhere in Ireland

definitions.text: May be taken out to have a drink
definitions.meaning: a bottle stopper is removed before drinking
a city and county in the south of Ireland

explanation.surface: An invitation to go out for a drink somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopper is pulled from a bottle before drinking; it is also Ireland's second city.

clue.text: Grass required to bring up herbivores

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing up means the letters run from bottom to top

parts.note: deer are plant-eating animals

explanation.surface: Grass is needed to rear plant-eating animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed is a tall grass that grows in wet places.

clue.text: Type a letter between R and U

definitions.text: a letter between R and U
definitions.meaning: the letters strictly between R and U in the alphabet are S and T, so the answer is one or the other

explanation.surface: Someone is told to key in a letter that falls between R and U.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two letters and a conjunction: one letter or the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a type is a kind or class of thing.

clue.text: As well as being no end luxurious

indicators.note: no end means the final letter is dropped from the luxurious word

parts.note: plush means luxurious

explanation.surface: Something is endlessly luxurious as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' usually means very much; here it removes the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: plus means in addition to, as in 'tax plus tip'.

clue.text: On the opposing side, meantime, getting me dismissed twice

indicators.note: dismissed means those letters are sent away from the word meantime
twice means the word me is taken two times

parts.note: me taken as written

explanation.surface: A player is sent off twice while their side is losing.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove ME from the start and the end of MEANTIME.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is against something is on the opposing side of the debate.

clue.text: Unable to tell a plum from an apricot

definitions.text: Unable to tell a plum from an apricot

parts.words: Unable to tell a plum from an apricot
parts.note: plum and apricot are also names of shades, so confusing them is a failure of colour vision rather than fruit knowledge

explanation.surface: Someone confuses two fruits at the greengrocer.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with defective colour vision cannot distinguish certain hues, like purplish plum and orange apricot.

clue.text: Proceed to arrest

definitions.meaning: to originate or derive, as in a problem that comes from a cause
to check or halt a flow, as of blood

explanation.surface: A police order to go ahead and make the arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem from is to proceed from a source; to stem bleeding is to arrest it.

clue.text: Mentioning in tenancy chit

parts.note: a letting is a property rented out, a tenancy
a chit is a slip of paper

explanation.surface: A rental document mentions something in passing.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to reveal something inadvertently is to mention it by accident.
